subject: electric kettle
title: What If a Whole Nation Boiled Its Kettles at Once? Britain Does, on Schedule

scenes.text: What if a whole nation boiled its kettles at once? Britain does, and the grid watches TV.
A British kettle pulls up to 3 kilowatts. When a hit show ends, millions click them on together and demand jumps 200 to 400 megawatts. Engineers call it TV pickup.
The record: 4 July 1990. England lost a World Cup penalty shootout, 26 million viewers stood up, and demand leapt 2,800 megawatts. About 933,000 kettles.
So National Grid studies the TV schedules and five years of demand data to predict each surge.
When it hits, a pumped-storage plant inside a Welsh mountain, Dinorwig, drops water through its turbines: 1,320 megawatts in 12 seconds.
Streaming has shrunk the surges, but big moments still land. The Queen's 2020 pandemic address: 500 to 600 megawatts of tea.

description:
What if millions of people switched on their kettles in the same minute? In Britain they do, every time a popular programme ends, and the grid plans for it.
TV pickup surges typically add 200 to 400 MW; the record was 2,800 MW after the 1990 World Cup semi-final penalty shootout, roughly 933,000 kettles. National Grid forecasts the surges from TV schedules and five years of demand data, and the Dinorwig pumped-storage station in Wales can deliver 1,320 MW within 12 seconds. Streaming has reduced the effect, but the Queen's 2020 pandemic address still caused a 500 to 600 MW pickup.
